Soylent Green. A nineteen seventy-three science-fiction film set in an overpopulated, resource-depleted future New York where the masses subsist on synthetic food.

The year is twenty twenty-two. Overpopulation has exhausted resources and the poor survive on government-issued wafers. Detective Frank Thorn, played by Charlton Heston, investigates the death of a corporate executive named Simonson. What begins as a routine murder investigation leads him deeper into a conspiracy that reaches the highest levels of government.

Through forensic investigation, Thorn discovers something horrifying. The government's Soylent Green food product, supposedly made from plant matter, contains human tissue. The plant matter in the formula matches human composition. The twist is discovered not through dramatic revelation but through scientific analysis. The most abundant variety of Soylent, color-coded green, is the secret product distributed to the poorest districts. The masses are unknowingly consuming their own.

Mortally wounded, Thorn learns the full truth. He cries out to the masses: Soylent Green is people. His desperate cry of revelation becomes the film's haunting final moment.

Directed by Richard Fleischer and loosely adapted from Harry Harrison's novel Make Room Make Room, the film critiques overpopulation, corporate greed, environmental collapse, and the devaluation of human dignity. The twist literalizes the reduction of human bodies to consumable product. The film uses science-fiction pessimism to condemn indifference to mass suffering. By making cannibalism involuntary and invisible, the film asks difficult questions about complicity and complicity in systems we do not see or understand. The twist serves not merely as a plot device but as social commentary on how industrial systems reduce human life to economic transactions and consumable commodities.
